hints: For step 1 look at what changes on the ring, benzene gains a $\text{CH}_3$ group, so think which electrophilic substitution adds an alkyl group and what carrier generates the electrophile.
For step 2 look at what changes on the side chain, $\text{CH}_3$ becomes $\text{COOH}$, so recall the strong oxidising agent that oxidises an alkyl side chain on a benzene ring completely.
walkthrough:
Spot step 1 as adding a methyl group to the ring**
You start with benzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, and end with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$. That is electrophilic substitution of H by $\text{CH}_3$. The classic way is Friedel-Crafts alkylation using chloromethane as the source of the electrophile: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCl}$$ $\text{AlCl}_3$ is the Lewis acid catalyst that polarises $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ to make $\text{CH}_3^+$ like electrophile.

Spot step 2 as complete oxidation of the side chain**
Now $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ becomes $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$. The benzene ring is very resistant to oxidation, but an alkyl side chain is oxidised right up to the benzoic acid stage. Use hot alkaline potassium manganate(VII), $\text{MnO}_4^-$, with heating, followed by dilute acid to protonate the benzoate ion to benzoic acid.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst
step 2: hot alkaline $\text{MnO}_4^-$ , heat, then acidify

hints: Count the carbon types in methylbenzene, one $\text{CH}_3$ carbon next to arene plus four different ring carbon environments due to symmetry, then match each type to Table 7.1.
Count the carbon types in benzoic acid, one $\text{COOH}$ carboxyl carbon plus four different ring carbon environments, then match each type to Table 7.1.
walkthrough:
Work out why there are five peaks in each molecule**
Both molecules are monosubstituted benzenes. The ring has a plane of symmetry through the substituent and the opposite carbon, so the 6 ring carbons give 4 different environments: the ipso carbon attached to the substituent, ortho (2 equivalent), meta (2 equivalent) and para (1). Add the one side chain carbon and you get 5 peaks in total.

Assign methylbenzene using Table 7.1**
The 4 ring carbons are $sp^2$ alkene or arene carbons, so Table 7.1 puts them at 110-160 ppm. The $\text{CH}_3$ carbon is $sp^3$ next to arene, $-\text{C}-\text{Ar}$, so it appears at 25-50 ppm. That gives 4 peaks at 110-160 and 1 peak at 25-50.

Assign benzoic acid using Table 7.1**
Again the 4 ring environments are $sp^2$ arene carbons at 110-160 ppm. The $\text{COOH}$ carbon is $sp^2$ carboxyl, $\text{R}-\text{COOH}$, so Table 7.1 puts it at 160-185 ppm. That gives 4 peaks at 110-160 and 1 peak at 160-185.

Final answer: methylbenzene: has 4 peak(s) in the chemical shift range of 110-160 and has 1 peak(s) in the chemical shift range of 25-50.
benzoic acid: has 4 peak(s) in the chemical shift range of 110-160 and has 1 peak(s) in the chemical shift range of 160-185.

hints: Both J and K have formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$, which is methylbenzene with one H replaced by one Cl, so think where that Cl could go, on the ring or on the side chain.
Recall that $\text{Cl}_2$ with a halogen carrier gives electrophilic substitution on the benzene ring, while $\text{Cl}_2$ with light gives a different mechanism.
Think about the directing effect of $\text{CH}_3$, it is 2,4 directing, so ring substitution gives mainly ortho and para isomers.
Draw the side chain product as $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ and link each type of product to its specific condition, $\text{AlCl}_3$ versus uv light.
walkthrough:
See two different places for Cl to go**
Methylbenzene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ plus $\text{Cl}_2$ to give $\text{C}_7\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$ means monosubstitution. The Cl can either replace a ring H to give $\text{ClC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_3$, or replace a side chain H to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Those are your J and K.

Draw the ring chlorination product**
$\text{CH}_3$ is an activating 2,4 directing group, so electrophilic substitution puts Cl ortho or para to the methyl group. Draw a benzene ring with $\text{CH}_3$ and Cl in 2 positions (ortho, 2-chloromethylbenzene) or in 4 positions (para, 4-chloromethylbenzene). Either is accepted.

Draw the side chain chlorination product**
Free radical substitution replaces one H of the $\text{CH}_3$ group. Draw a benzene ring attached to $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. This is phenylmethyl chloride, also called benzyl chloride: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{uv} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$

Match conditions to mechanism**
Ring substitution is electrophilic and needs $\text{Cl}_2$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$ carrier to generate $\text{Cl}^+$. Side chain substitution is free radical and needs $\text{Cl}_2$ with uv light to generate $\text{Cl}$ radicals by homolytic fission. That is why the question stresses different conditions with different reagents.

Final answer: J and K in either order: 2-chloromethylbenzene or 4-chloromethylbenzene [ring with $\text{CH}_3$ and Cl ortho or para] and phenylmethyl chloride $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ [ring with $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ substituent].
to form ring substituted product: $\text{Cl}_2$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$.
to form side-chain substituted product: $\text{Cl}_2$ with uv light.

hints: Compare formulas, benzoic acid is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$, L is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{ClO}_2$ so one ring H is replaced by Cl, while M is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{ClO}$ so $\text{OH}$ is replaced by Cl.
Recall the directing effect of $\text{COOH}$, it is a deactivating 3,5 directing group, so think where electrophilic chlorination of the ring will occur.
Recall which reagents convert a $\text{COOH}$ group into a $\text{COCl}$ group without touching the ring, and why $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_5$ are chosen.
walkthrough:
Deduce L as ring chlorination**
L keeps both O atoms ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{ClO}_2$), so the $\text{COOH}$ group is intact and Cl has replaced a ring H. $\text{COOH}$ is deactivating and meta directing, so electrophilic substitution gives the 3 isomer. Draw a benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ and Cl in meta positions. This is 3-chlorobenzoic acid.

Deduce M as acyl chloride formation**
M has only one O ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{ClO}$), so $\text{OH}$ of the acid has been replaced by Cl. Draw a benzene ring attached to $\text{C}=\text{O}$ attached to Cl: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$$ This is benzoyl chloride. The ring is untouched.

Choose the reagent for M**
Carboxylic acid to acyl chloride needs a chlorinating agent for the $\text{OH}$ group. Use $\text{SOCl}_2$, or $\text{PCl}_5$, or $\text{PCl}_3$ with heat. For example: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$$ Do not confuse this with $\text{Cl}_2$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$, which would attack the ring to give L.

Final answer: L: 3-chlorobenzoic acid [benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ and Cl meta to each other].
M: benzoyl chloride [benzene ring with $\text{COCl}$ substituent, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$].
to form M: $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ with heat.
